questions.answer:
```c
return (int *) &arr[index];
```

or equivalently `return (int *) (arr + index);`
questions.grading: Essential: return the *address* of the maximum element, i.e. `&arr[index]` or `arr + index`. The `(int *)` cast is needed only because `arr` is `const int *` and the return type is `int *`; without it gcc compiles the code but warns "return discards 'const' qualifier". Give full marks with or without the cast (the course didn't stress this). Wrong: `return arr[index];` (returns the value, not a pointer: 0 marks), `return *arr + index;`, `return &hi;` (address of a local variable, dangling once the function returns: 0 marks), `return arr;` (pointer to the first element).


questions.source: Final exam April 2022, Q5(a)
questions.answer: No (not reliably). The generic stack stores only the **pointer** `&z`, not a copy of the value. `z` is a local variable with automatic storage duration, so its lifetime ends when `push_zero` returns. The top node then holds a dangling pointer to memory that no longer belongs to `z`; reading through it is undefined behaviour and the memory will likely be overwritten by later function calls. (Fix: push a pointer to heap memory, e.g. `double *z = malloc(sizeof *z); *z = 0.0; stack_push(s, z);`.)
questions.grading: Typo on the paper: the prose says `stack_push(void *elem)` but the call is `stack_push(s, &z)`; the intended signature takes the stack too — irrelevant to the answer. 1 mark for "no / not guaranteed / undefined" and 1 for the reason: the stack stores the address of a local variable whose lifetime ends when the function returns (dangling pointer). Accept "it might still read 0 by chance, but it is undefined behaviour". "Yes" earns 0 even with a reason; "No" with a wrong reason (e.g. "because 0.0 is a double, not an int" or "void pointers can't hold doubles") earns 1 at most.

rubric.item: Answers no (or: not guaranteed / undefined behaviour)
Explains the stack stores a pointer to the local variable z, which no longer exists after push_zero returns (dangling pointer)

questions.source: Variant of Final exam April 2022, Q5(a)
questions.answer: Yes. The stack stores the pointer `p`, which points to memory on the **heap**. Heap memory allocated with `malloc` stays valid until it is explicitly `free`d, so it outlives the call to `push_one`; only the local pointer variable `p` disappears, and its value (the address) has already been copied into the stack's node. The element therefore still holds 1. (Whoever pops it later is responsible for freeing it.)
questions.grading: 1 mark for "yes", 1 for the reason: the pointer refers to heap memory, which persists after the function returns until freed (contrast with a local variable, whose lifetime ends). Answering "no because p is a local variable" confuses the pointer variable with the memory it points to: 0. Mentioning that the caller must eventually free the element is good but not required.

rubric.item: Answers yes
Explains that malloc'd heap memory remains valid after the function returns (only the local pointer variable goes away; its value was copied into the stack)

questions.source: Final exam April 2022, Q6(a)
questions.prompt:
**Question 6(a) (10 points)**

Write the following C function:

```c
int read_strings(const char* filename, char *s[static 100])
```

that opens the file having name `filename`, reads the contents of the file, and then closes the file. Assume that the file exists, is readable, and consists of an unspecified number of lines where each line is a string. The function should read each line of the file and store each line in the array `s` (the contents of the first line of the file should be stored in `s[0]`, the second line in `s[1]`, and so on). You should assume that `s[i]` has sufficient capacity to store the contents of line `i` (i.e., do not dynamically allocate memory in this question). The function should return the number of lines read from the file. If there are more than 100 lines in the file, then the function should store only the first 100 lines but still return the actual number of lines in the file.
questions.grading:
Essentials: `fopen(filename, "r")`; a loop that reads one line at a time until end of file (`fgets(...) != NULL`, `getline`, or `fgetc` until `EOF`); store line i in `s[i]` (copy characters into the existing buffer: `fgets` directly into `s[n]`, or `strcpy(s[n], buf)`); only store when `n < 100` but keep counting afterwards (read later lines into a scratch buffer); `fclose`; return the count.

Accepted: keeping or stripping the newline (either is fine if consistent with 6(d)); an assumed buffer size for `fgets` (the question gives none, so any reasonable constant like 100, 1000 or `BUFSIZ` is fine); `fscanf(f, "%[^\n]\n", ...)`-style reading if it handles lines correctly. No error checking needed (file is assumed readable).

Common mistakes: `s[n] = buf;` (stores the same buffer pointer in every element, so all lines end up equal: lose 3); stopping at 100 lines instead of counting the rest (lose 2); writing to `s[100]` or beyond (lose 2); using `fscanf("%s")` (stops at spaces, so it reads words not lines: lose 2–3); forgetting `fclose` (lose 1); `malloc`ing the strings (the question forbids it: lose 1); `char c` instead of `int c` with `fgetc` (minor, lose at most 1); counting a trailing empty line when the file ends with a newline.

rubric.item: Opens the file with fopen(filename, "r")
Correct loop that reads the file one line at a time until end of file
Stores line i into s[i] by copying into the existing storage (not by assigning a shared buffer pointer)
Stores only the first 100 lines but keeps counting the rest; no access past s[99]
Closes the file with fclose
Returns the total number of lines in the file

questions.prompt:
**Question 6(b) (10 points)**

Write the following C function:

```c
void shortest_to_front(int n, char *s[static n])
```

that finds the shortest string in the array `s` and moves the shortest string to the front of the array by swapping the shortest string with the string at the front of the array. For example, if `s` is the array `["zebra", "anteater", "bat", "frog"]` then calling the function would modify `s` so that it becomes the array `["bat", "anteater", "zebra", "frog"]`.
questions.grading:
Essentials: find the index (or a pointer to the element) of the shortest string with a loop and `strlen`; then swap the two `char *` pointers `s[0]` and `s[min]` through a temporary. Ties may go to any of the shortest strings. Accept a `char **` pointer to the minimum element, a loop starting at 0, or computing lengths into a variable.

Common mistakes: swapping string contents with `strcpy` (the strings may have different capacities, e.g. copying "anteater" into the 6-byte "zebra" storage overflows; lose 2–3); swapping without a temporary (`s[0] = s[min]; s[min] = s[0];` loses a string: lose 2); comparing strings with `strcmp` (alphabetical, not length: lose 3); comparing `sizeof(s[i])` (size of a pointer, always 8: lose 3); tracking the minimum length but not its index, so the swap can't be done; off-by-one loop bounds (`i <= n`).

rubric.item: Correct header and loop over all n strings
Uses strlen to compare string lengths

questions.prompt:
**Question 6(c) (2 points)**

Write the following C function:

```c
void sort_by_length(int n, char *s[static n])
```

that sorts the array of strings `s` in increasing string length using the `shortest_to_front` function from Question 6(b). For example, if `s` is the array `["zebra", "anteater", "bat", "frog"]` then calling the function would modify `s` so that it becomes the array `["bat", "frog", "zebra", "anteater"]`. To move elements of the array `s`, you must use the `shortest_to_front` function (this means that you cannot write something like `s[i] = …` to assign an array element).

Hint: Call `shortest_to_front` (n-1) times. You don't need to answer 6(b) to use `shortest_to_front` in your answer.

For reference, Question 6(b) was: write `void shortest_to_front(int n, char *s[static n])` that finds the shortest string in the array `s` and moves it to the front of the array by swapping it with the string at the front of the array (e.g. `["zebra", "anteater", "bat", "frog"]` becomes `["bat", "anteater", "zebra", "frog"]`).
questions.grading: Essential idea: call `shortest_to_front` n-1 times on shrinking sub-arrays: `shortest_to_front(n - i, s + i)` or `shortest_to_front(n - i, &s[i])` (taking an address is not an assignment, so `&s[i]` is allowed). Running i to n-1 (one extra call on a 1-element sub-array) is harmless. Deductions: calling `shortest_to_front(n, s)` repeatedly on the whole array (does nothing after the first call: 0–1); passing `s + i` but keeping length `n` (reads past the end of the array: lose 1); assigning `s[i] = ...` (forbidden).

Passes the shrinking sub-array correctly: s + i (or &s[i]) with length n - i
